research.job_description_summary: Wipro's official early-careers page lists the Elite programme (newly graduated engineers) and the Turbo programme (engineering talent from 46 named institutes, including IIITs and NITs), among others, but gives no selection stages or skills. Secondary sources describe the National Level Talent Hunt (NLTH) online test (aptitude, essay, and per one source a coding section), followed by a technical and an HR interview. Elite is described as the Project Engineer track (about 3.5 LPA) and Turbo as a higher track.
required_skills: Programming fundamentals (C, C++, Java or Python)
limitations: The official Wipro early-careers page names the programmes but describes no selection stages, exam pattern or required skills; a sample official Project Engineer posting (2025) is for a mechanical design role and is not relevant to fresher software hiring.

Sources disagree on the NLTH pattern: one guide says aptitude plus an essay and two coding questions, another says aptitude (about 20 questions, 60 minutes) plus an essay with coding only in the technical interview. Coding rounds are therefore labeled REPORTED.

The Unstop article (updated 2026-03-06) and the JobRise guide (2026-02-11) are editorial lists; their questions are not attributed to individual candidates, so most items here are original practice questions (class D) using those lists as topic context.
Only two items come from explicitly attributed candidate anecdotes inside the JobRise guide (a HashMap question and a Java memory-model question); each is a single report.
The 15-month service agreement, package figures, cutoffs and the Turbo role title (Senior Project Engineer) come from secondary sources and were not confirmed on Wipro's own pages.
Turbo hiring is restricted to named institutes, so Turbo content may not apply to all candidates.

Evidence handling: practice questions cite no sources; where a source only supplied topic context it is named in the question notes. Practice and job-description-inferred questions are UNVERIFIED and capped at LOW confidence on import.

Review status: answers, samples and cited counts come from the researcher and were not independently re-run; spot checks only. Source titles and some dates are blank because the sources did not show them.

mcq.explanation: Together they do 4 x (1/15 + 1/20) = 7/15 of the job. Remaining 8/15 at B's rate of 1/20 per day = 32/3 = 10 2/3 days.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between synchronized and volatile in Java.
questions.relevance_to_role: A secondary source says Wipro Turbo uses the same online test with a higher cutoff and a harder technical interview.
questions.expected_answer: volatile guarantees visibility of a variable across threads (and ordering) but not atomicity of compound actions. synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility for a block; use it (or atomics) for read-modify-write operations.
follow_ups: Is count++ safe on a volatile int?

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
questions.relevance_to_role: A secondary source says Wipro Turbo uses the same online test with a higher cutoff and a harder technical interview.
questions.expected_answer: A clustered index defines the physical order of rows (one per table). A non-clustered index is a separate structure with pointers to rows (many per table). Clustered is faster for range scans on the key; non-clustered needs lookups.
follow_ups: Why can only one clustered index exist?
common_mistakes: Saying both store rows in order

questions.prompt: Compare a monolithic application with microservices. When would you avoid microservices?
questions.relevance_to_role: A secondary source says Wipro Turbo uses the same online test with a higher cutoff and a harder technical interview.
questions.expected_answer: A monolith is one deployable unit: simple to build and test but scales and changes together. Microservices split by business capability for independent deployment and scaling but add network, data-consistency and operational complexity. Avoid them for small teams or early-stage products.
